notes: Exact CompareNumbers in helpers.go is wired into Eq, compareGet and Where; the old numeric code in where.go stays in place as mostly-dead fallback and reflect.ValueOf is called twice in compareGet; tests are broad (hreflect unit, Where, and integration).

Correct exact comparison wired into Eq, compareGet and the where comparison operators, with non-comparison operators falling through to the old code; it leaves the now-stale lossy numeric branches in where.go in place, though they are harmless.

CompareNumbers is exact, and Eq, compareGet and Where all use it; the old float64 numeric code in where.go is left behind as near-dead code, and `return 0, float64(-c)` is a cryptic way to encode the result.

Mirrors the reference structure and is correct, including NaN fallthrough in where; the `return 0, float64(-c)` encoding in compareGet is a bit cryptic and there is no direct unit test of CompareNumbers, though coverage through doTestCompare is extensive.

Correct exact comparison with explicit NaN handling in both compareGet and Where; the rewritten `else if !IsNumber||!IsNumber` branch is awkward and the same-kind numeric cases are left dead; tests are strong, including a reverse-symmetry unit test and a check that all six functions agree.

Correct and well tested (symmetry checks plus all six operators in both directions); the where else-if guard that preserves old fallthrough behaviour and the reliance on math.MaxInt64 rounding to 2^63 are slightly awkward but commented.

Cleanest where.go change, removing the old float64 paths and routing numbers through checkNumberCondition with NaN semantics; it reinvents cmp.Compare as cmp3 and repeats the list of non-comparison operators; tests are thorough, though the integration test uses an invalid kind name ('robots').

Exact CompareNumbers is used in Eq, compareGet and a dedicated where helper, and the old lossy numeric branches are removed cleanly; minor nits are a hand-rolled cmp3 in place of cmp.Compare and a hardcoded list of non-comparison operators in checkNumberCondition that could drift from the main switch.

The fix is equivalent to the reference but tracks each segment and releases refs only after WBL truncation; the test is thorough and checks checkpoint contents across restarts, yet the package suite failed and the per-sample mutex in the replay loop is a minor inefficiency.

The fix is sound. It records WBL-referenced duplicate refs per segment, keeps them in the checkpoint, and drops them on WBL truncation, which is equivalent to and slightly more precise than the reference. It does add a per-sample mutex lock in the replay loop. The package suite failed, most likely because its own checkpoint-content assertions fail.

It batches duplicate refs per segment like the reference, gets the segment from r.Segment() without changing the loadWBL signature, and releases refs on WBL truncation; the full-lifecycle test passes, and the only small gap is that it skips pinning when decodeErr is set.

This closely mirrors the reference: duplicate refs are collected per segment and registered once, they are kept in the checkpoint, and segment-wise release happens on WBL truncation. Using r.Segment() avoids a signature change. The only gap is that refs are not pinned when a decode error occurs. The thorough restart test passes.
The logic is correct, with clean helper methods (update/get/truncateWBLExpiries) and a reasonable reproduction test, but it locks for every sample during replay and the package suite failed.

The implementation is correct and has clean helpers: a per-segment WBL expiry checked in keepSeriesInWALCheckpointFn and released after WBL truncation. Locking per sample is acceptable. The package suite failed, probably because its own test asserts WAL expiry details too tightly.

The fix is sound: it pins duplicate WBL refs per segment and releases them once the WBL is truncated, but it takes the mutex for every sample, and its own test appears broken because the final db.Compact will not run OOO compaction when the head is not compactable, so require.Empty(wblExpiries) fails, consistent with the failed package suite.

The fix works and is functionally the same as the others. The loadWBL parameter order is reshuffled, and truncateOOO manipulates the map inline. The test pokes at the internal map under the mutex and depends on full db.Compact scheduling, and the package suite failed.

Reuses a refactored split helper, but that helper only assigns the internal issuer when public and internal names are mixed, so a list like `localhost` or `127.0.0.1` alone gets a policy that consolidation drops, and with no http app these names fall back to ACME, violating the internal-issuer requirement; its tests never cover this case.

Clean refactor and good site-block/auto_https-off handling. It only assigns the internal issuer when public and internal names are mixed, so a list of only internal names (e.g. just localhost) gets no explicit internal policy, violating an explicit requirement; its tests miss this case.

Correctly forces automation, skips site-block names, and gives all-internal lists an explicit internal issuer through a refactored helper with an `explicitInternal` flag; it adds unasked-for lowercasing and still emits noise policies for public names without global options, but has a good unit test plus four adapt tests.

Functionally close: it tracks site-block subjects, forces internal issuer for internal-only names, and applies renewal_window_ratio. It rewires the site-block path through a boolean-flag helper and lowercases names, emits noise policies unlike the reference, and its no_sites golden file looks inconsistent with how consolidation keeps empty public policies.

Functionally covers every spec point: append parsing, automate loader with auto_https off, site-block policy wins, and an internal issuer even for all-internal lists; but it duplicates the existing public/internal split logic, validates names redundantly in the parser, passes warnings by value so they can be lost, and emits empty subject-only policies that the reference avoids (likely why the hidden test fails).

A self-contained helper builds public and internal policies for uncovered names without touching existing code. It handles internal-only names and site-block precedence, but duplicates the split logic, validates subjects redundantly at parse time, and still emits empty public policies that diverge from the expected output.

Sound implementation: it reuses an extracted split helper, checks all existing policies for overlap, adds names to the loader unconditionally, and explicitly assigns the internal issuer to all-internal lists; the internal-issuer check is a bit convoluted, it emits empty subject-only policies unlike the reference, and its four adapt tests cover the main scenarios well.

Covers the spec: names are appended to automate, site-block policies win via a subject check, and internal names get the internal issuer (both mixed and internal-only cases). It always emits a subject policy for public names, even an empty one, so its adapt output differs from the expected golden output; the extracted split helper is a reasonable refactor.

Passes the hidden test and the full package suite, but it decides which chunks to keep by time against the new reference's earliest chunk: OOO chunks written under the live reference with timestamps before that point are still dropped (data loss), kept OOO chunks are not re-sorted by disk ref as truncation requires, and without lastMmapRef it keeps chunks written during replay when the new reference has none.

It is concise and passes every test, but keeps existing chunks only when maxTime >= the new ref's earliest chunk time. Valid OOO chunks older than that are dropped (data loss in a natural variant of the issue), and the merged OOO list is not sorted by ref.

Keeping chunks whose disk ref is newer than the new reference's chunks is reasonable, but it ignores lastMmapRef, keeps all history when the new reference has no chunks, edits an unrelated existing test's OOO window, uses exact sample equality that may be fragile for histograms, and the suite fails.

Ref- and time-based retention handles the main scenario and keeps OOO chunks in ref order. It does not discard chunks written during the current replay when the other ref has no chunks, it edits an unrelated existing test's OOO window, and the package suite fails.

Closest in spirit to the reference: keeps on-disk chunks between the new reference's first chunk and lastMmapRef, dedupes, sorts OOO by ref and in-order by time, and has clean helpers and a good test (OOO samples older than the new reference), yet it omits the gc minMmapFile fix and the package suite fails.

The approach is close to the reference: it threads lastMmapRef through, merges in-order chunks by time, unions OOO chunks sorted by ref, and drops pre-new-ref history by disk order. It omits the gc minMmapFile fix, changes chunk counter semantics, and existing package tests regress.

Threads lastMmapRef through and uses a disk-ref boundary for OOO chunks, which is the right idea, but it adds a deferred per-sample cleanup to the hot replay loop, an O(n²) overlap resolver and reworked metric semantics, and the package suite fails.

It adds a complex deferred cleanup that drops in-order chunks ending before the next replayed sample, and changes the function's return signature. With WAL gaps or corruption this can discard healthy chunks, which repeats one of the issue's failure modes, and the package suite fails.
